terms.gloss: halfway, in the middle of the journey
terms.grammar: ablative; ex mediō itinere, “from halfway”, of turning back
evidence: Caes. BC 1.59: procul equitātū vīsō ex mediō itinere prōjectīs sarcinīs fugiēbant
terms.comment: Caesar’s phrase, of foragers who dropped their packs halfway along and ran. For “we’re halfway there”, say how much of the way is done: dīmidium viae cōnfēcimus, as Pliny measures half a distance as dīmidium spatiī (NH 2.84).

terms.grammar: with the genitive or the dative of the two places
evidence: Caes. BG 1.34.1: utī aliquem locum medium utrīsque conloquiō dēligeret
Caes. BG 4.19: hunc esse dēlēctum medium ferē regiōnum eārum

phrases.latin: Jam dīmidium viae cōnfēcimus; mox apud aviam erimus.
phrases.english: We’re halfway there now; soon we’ll be at Grandma’s.

phrases.latin: aut aliquō acceptō dētrīmentō aut procul equitātū vīsō ex mediō itinere prōjectīs sarcinīs fugiēbant
phrases.english: either after some loss, or on seeing our cavalry in the distance, they would drop their packs halfway along the road and run

phrases.latin: utī aliquem locum medium utrīsque conloquiō dēligeret
phrases.english: that he should choose some place halfway between them for a talk

sources: Lewis & Short: medius · Lewis & Short: dimidium
